summary: Sets requirements for NATs that handle TCP, so that applications such as peer-to-peer software and online games can work consistently through them. This is a Best Current Practice, later updated by RFC 7857.

eli5.summary: A mail room that relabels packages can make life hard for people trying to reach each other. These rules tell the mail room how to behave so connections still work.

questions: how should a nat handle tcp connections
what are the nat requirements for tcp
how long should a nat keep idle tcp connections
subtitle: Ten rules for NATs so that peer-to-peer apps and games can open TCP connections through them.

tldr.problem: NATs get in the way of applications that need connections started toward internal hosts, and NATs that mishandle details of TCP force peer-to-peer software to fall back on public relays.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists ten numbered requirements (REQ-1 to REQ-10) covering mapping and filtering behavior, TCP simultaneous-open, idle timeouts, application level gateways, port assignment, hairpinning and ICMP handling.
tldr.outcome: A NAT that follows the MUST requirements and the UDP requirements is compliant, which raises the odds that NAT traversal works without relays. The RFC is a Best Current Practice, updated by RFC 7857.

today: RFC 5382 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 142) and has been updated by RFC 7857. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Scope and Purpose
sections.content:
RFC 5382 is an adjunct to the UDP NAT requirements in RFC 4787, which defines most NAT terms and sets general requirements. This document sets requirements for NATs that handle TCP. It applies to traditional NATs as described in RFC 2663, and it inherits all definitions and requirements from RFC 4787.

It covers only the TCP side of NAT traversal. Firewalls, packet inspection above TCP, signaling-based approaches such as MIDCOM and UPnP, and connections to or from the NAT itself are out of scope.

The motivation is that traversal techniques for peer-to-peer TCP depend on NAT behavior that is usually, but not always, present. When it is missing, a traversal solution must use public TCP relays. The requirements aim to make such relays unnecessary.
sections.eli5: These rules are only about one kind of connection, TCP, and only about how the mail room treats it, not about guards or locks.

sections.title: Mapping and Connection Initiation
sections.content:
A NAT keeps a mapping that translates the addresses and ports of each connection. Take an internal endpoint (X:x) that connects to external (Y1:y1) and gets mapping (X1':x1'), then connects from the same (X:x) to (Y2:y2) and gets (X2':x2'). If the two mappings are equal for all (Y2:y2), the NAT has Endpoint-Independent Mapping. If equal only when Y2 equals Y1, it is Address-Dependent. This RFC adds Connection-Dependent Mapping, where a new mapping is allocated for every connection.

REQ-1: a NAT MUST have Endpoint-Independent Mapping for TCP. That lets a peer learn and advertise its external address and port so others can reach it, without weakening the NAT's security policy.

Peers that sit behind NATs often use simultaneous-open: both send a SYN for the same connection, the SYNs cross, and each answers with a SYN-ACK. Some NATs wrongly block the inbound SYN or mangle the outbound SYN-ACK. REQ-2: a NAT MUST support all valid sequences of TCP packets from RFC 793, including simultaneous-open in addition to the 3-way handshake.
sections.eli5: The mail room should always give the same return address to the same kid, and it must let two kids start a call to each other at the same moment.

sections.title: Externally Initiated Connections and Unsolicited SYNs
sections.content:
When an outside host sends a SYN to an existing mapping, the NAT can allow it or filter it. Filtering behaviors are Endpoint-Independent (allow anyone), Address-Dependent (only the address already contacted), Address and Port-Dependent, and the new Connection-Dependent (allow nothing from outside). REQ-3: for application transparency, Endpoint-Independent Filtering is RECOMMENDED; if stricter filtering matters more, Address-Dependent Filtering is RECOMMENDED. It MAY be configurable, and MAY differ from UDP's.

If an inbound SYN is filtered, the NAT can drop it silently or send an error. Silence helps simultaneous-open, because the outside host retransmits the SYN after the delayed outbound SYN has created the mapping. Errors such as TCP RST or ICMP Port Unreachable make the sender give up.

REQ-4 is the compromise: a NAT MUST NOT respond to an unsolicited inbound SYN for at least 6 seconds. If it sees and translates a matching outbound SYN in that time, it MUST silently drop the original. Otherwise it SHOULD send ICMP Port Unreachable (Type 3, Code 3), unless that would violate its security policy, in which case it MUST drop silently.
sections.eli5: If a stranger knocks before you have opened your own door, wait a few seconds before answering. Maybe you were just about to open it yourself.

sections.title: Session Refresh and Idle Timeouts
sections.content:
A NAT holds state for each connection and can be attacked by exhausting it, so it must be able to abandon sessions. The RFC describes three connection phases: partially open, established, and closing. Established connections can stay idle indefinitely, so no single timeout suits everyone. Hosts may send keep-alives, by default every 2 hours, and partially open or closing connections can idle for at most 4 minutes.

REQ-5: if a NAT cannot tell whether endpoints are active, it MAY abandon an idle session, but the established connection idle-timeout MUST NOT be less than 2 hours 4 minutes, and the transitory idle-timeout MUST NOT be less than 4 minutes. Timeouts MAY be configurable.

Several behaviors are left unspecified: handling of RST packets, how to treat connections in TIME_WAIT, what to do with non-SYN packets that have no mapping (drop or send RST), and whether to send RST when abandoning a live connection.
sections.eli5: The mail room should not throw away a quiet conversation too early. Waiting a bit over two hours means a friend's regular check-in message will still find its way.

sections.title: ALGs, Ports, Hairpinning and ICMP
sections.content:
REQ-6: application level gateways that affect TCP are RECOMMENDED to be disabled by default, except for FTP, because legacy FTP clients often do not enable passive mode and need the ALG.

REQ-7: a NAT MUST NOT use port overloading for TCP, so two internal endpoints can both reach the same external endpoint. REQ-8: a NAT MUST support hairpinning for TCP, presenting the packet with the external source address and port, so two hosts behind the same NAT can reach each other by their external addresses.

REQ-9: a NAT SHOULD translate ICMP Destination Unreachable (Type 3) messages, which path MTU discovery needs. REQ-10: receiving any ICMP message MUST NOT terminate the NAT mapping or TCP connection it concerns, which matters when a remote NAT briefly signals an error during simultaneous-open.
sections.eli5: Do not let helpers rewrite the notes inside, let friends in the same house reach each other, and do not hang up a call just because one small warning arrived.

sections.title: Compliance and Security
sections.content:
A NAT that meets every MUST and complies with RFC 4787 is compliant. One that also meets the RECOMMENDED items is fully compliant with the mandatory and recommended requirements.

Security notes address each requirement. For REQ-3, Connection-Dependent Filtering is most secure but severely restricts connection initiation. Endpoint-Independent Filtering requires an attacker to guess an active mapping's address and port. Address-Dependent Filtering also requires guessing the external endpoint's address, though it does not protect against attacks from behind a remote NAT with a single address that also carries a legitimate connection to the victim.

For REQ-4, an ICMP error may reveal the NAT to an attacker, while silent dropping hinders diagnosis, so implementers must weigh the options. NATs that modify sequence numbers must handle SACK properly, and those that change state from TCP flags must handle out-of-window packets.
sections.eli5: Stricter rules keep more strangers out but also keep out friends, so the mail room has to pick a balance.

items.label: Endpoint-Independent
items.desc: Allows initiations from all external endpoints.

items.label: Address-Dependent
items.desc: Allows only when the external address matches the one first contacted.

items.label: Address and Port-Dependent
items.desc: Allows only the same address and port, shortly after the first connection ends.

items.label: Connection-Dependent
items.desc: Allows no connection initiations from outside.
